find: During the Lower Palaeozoic (Cambrian to Devonian, roughly 540–360 million years ago), what is now Britain sat in the southern hemisphere tropics or subtropics, so warm-water carbonates and reef limestones are found in Wales and Scotland from this era.
replace: During the Lower Palaeozoic (Cambrian to Silurian, roughly 540–420 million years ago), what is now Britain lay in the southern hemisphere and drifted north from high southern latitudes into the subtropics, so warm-water carbonates and reef limestones are found in Wales and Scotland from the later part of this era.
note: F1: Lower Palaeozoic ends with the Silurian, not the Devonian; Britain was not tropical throughout it.

expect: A geologist finds a sequence of rocks in Wales that includes Carboniferous Limestone overlain by Carboniferous tillite. Explain what this sequence tells us about the change in climate during the Carboniferous period.
value: A geologist logs a sequence of rocks in southern Africa in which warm-water limestone is overlain by tillite. Explain what this sequence tells us about the change in climate during the Carboniferous.
note: F2: there is no Carboniferous tillite in Wales; Britain was equatorial then. Moved the scenario to Gondwana, where such sequences exist.

expect:
Mastering: Identifies that the limestone below indicates earlier warm, shallow marine greenhouse conditions; the tillite above indicates a shift to icehouse conditions with glaciation; cross-cutting relationships show the change was from warmer to colder, linking to the southward position of Gondwana and the growth of polar ice sheets.
Secure: Identifies both rock types and links each to greenhouse/icehouse conditions; explains the sequence as a climate cooling event.
Developing: Identifies one rock type correctly with the correct climate; does not fully develop the change or the sequence.
Emerging: States that the sequence shows climate change without linking rock types to conditions. [3 marks]
value:
Mastering: Identifies that the limestone below indicates earlier warm, shallow marine greenhouse conditions; the tillite above indicates a shift to icehouse conditions with glaciation; superposition shows the change was from warmer to colder, linking to the position of Gondwana over the South Pole and the growth of polar ice sheets.
Secure: Identifies both rock types and links each to greenhouse/icehouse conditions; explains the sequence as a climate cooling event.
Developing: Identifies one rock type correctly with the correct climate; does not fully develop the change or the sequence.
Emerging: States that the sequence shows climate change without linking rock types to conditions. [3 marks]
note: F2: a limestone-tillite sequence is dated by superposition, not cross-cutting relationships; Gondwana sat over the South Pole.
